questions.passageTitle: Mengapa Remaja Sulit Tidur Lebih Awal?
questions.passage: Banyak remaja sulit tidur sebelum tengah malam, lalu mengantuk berat di kelas pagi. Penjelasan ilmiahnya terletak pada jam biologis tubuh. Selama masa pubertas, hormon melatonin, yang memicu rasa kantuk, dilepaskan lebih lambat daripada pada anak-anak atau orang dewasa. Akibatnya, remaja cenderung baru merasa mengantuk pada malam hari yang lebih larut. Cahaya biru dari layar ponsel memperparah keadaan karena menekan produksi melatonin. Para peneliti menyarankan agar remaja mengurangi penggunaan layar satu jam sebelum tidur dan menjaga jam tidur yang konsisten. Selain itu, sebagian peneliti mengusulkan jam masuk sekolah yang lebih siang, tetapi usulan ini masih diperdebatkan karena berdampak pada jadwal transportasi dan pekerjaan orang tua.

questions.passageTitle: Cara Membuat Kompos Rumah Tangga (Teks Prosedur)
questions.passage:
**Bahan:** sisa sayur dan buah, daun kering, tanah, air, dan ember berlubang di bagian bawah.
**Langkah:**
1. Cacah sisa sayur dan buah menjadi potongan kecil.
2. Lapisi dasar ember dengan daun kering setebal tiga sentimeter.
3. Tambahkan cacahan sisa sayur, lalu tutup dengan selapis tanah.
4. Percikkan air hingga lembap, tetapi jangan sampai becek.
5. Aduk campuran seminggu sekali agar udara dapat masuk.
6. Setelah empat sampai enam minggu, kompos siap dipakai jika berwarna cokelat gelap dan tidak berbau busuk.

Jangan memasukkan daging, tulang, atau minyak karena dapat mendatangkan hewan pengganggu.

questions.passageTitle: Belajar dengan Bantuan Kecerdasan Buatan (Esai Argumentasi)
questions.passage: Kecerdasan buatan kini dapat menjawab soal dalam hitungan detik. Sebagian guru khawatir pelajar akan berhenti berpikir. Kekhawatiran itu masuk akal, tetapi larangan total bukanlah jawaban. Sebuah survei internal di satu sekolah menunjukkan bahwa 62 persen pelajar memakai alat bantu digital untuk memahami materi, sedangkan hanya 18 persen yang menyalin jawaban begitu saja. Angka ini menandakan bahwa sebagian besar pelajar memanfaatkannya sebagai pendamping belajar. Oleh karena itu, sekolah sebaiknya mengajarkan etika dan cara memeriksa kebenaran jawaban, bukan sekadar melarang. Pelajar perlu dibiasakan bertanya, "Dari mana jawaban ini berasal, dan apakah benar?"

Sekolah sebaiknya membimbing pemanfaatan yang bijak, bukan melarang total.

questions.passageTitle: Terumbu Karang yang Memutih (Artikel Ilmiah Populer)
questions.passage: Terumbu karang sering disebut hutan hujan lautan karena menyokong sekitar seperempat kehidupan laut, meskipun luasnya kurang dari satu persen dasar laut. Karang hidup bersimbiosis dengan alga kecil bernama zooxanthellae yang memberinya warna dan sebagian besar energi. Ketika suhu laut naik beberapa derajat di atas normal, karang mengeluarkan alga tersebut sehingga tampak memutih. Peristiwa pemutihan ini belum berarti karang mati, tetapi jika suhu tinggi bertahan lama, karang kelaparan dan akhirnya mati. Para ilmuwan mendorong pengurangan emisi karbon dan pengelolaan perikanan yang berkelanjutan sebagai langkah melindungi terumbu.

questions.passageTitle: The Return of the Javan Gibbon
questions.passage: Deep in the cloud forests of West Java lives the Javan gibbon, one of the rarest primates on Earth. Fewer than 4,000 individuals remain, mostly in small forest patches cut off from one another by farms and roads. Gibbons rarely come down to the ground, so a gap in the tree canopy can trap a family group in one area. To solve this problem, conservationists have begun building rope bridges between isolated patches. At first, the animals ignored them. After several months, however, a young female crossed one, and others soon followed. Researchers say the bridges are not a complete solution, but they give the species a chance to find mates and food beyond their small territories.

questions.passageTitle: The Surprising History of the Pencil
questions.passage: The pencil seems like a simple tool, but its history is full of surprises. In the 1500s, shepherds in England discovered a soft black mineral that left marks on their sheep. It was later named graphite, although people at first thought it was a type of lead, which explains why we still say "pencil lead". Because graphite was soft and dirty, early writers wrapped it in string or sheepskin. Later, craftsmen in Italy hollowed out wooden sticks and placed graphite inside, creating the pencil we know today. The eraser came much later: for years, people rubbed their mistakes away with bread. It was only in the 1770s that a scientist discovered that natural rubber could rub out pencil marks.

questions.passageTitle: A Letter to My Future Self
questions.passage:
Dear Me,
By the time you read this, you will have finished high school. I am writing in March, three weeks before the final exam, and I am tired. The pile of books on my desk is taller than my lamp, and my mother keeps bringing me tea that I forget to drink. But tonight, I made a promise, and I want you to remember it. I promise that whatever the results are, you will be proud of how hard you tried. I also promise that you will call Grandma more often, because she is the one who taught me to read. Whatever you have become, please do not forget the girl who studied by candlelight when the power went out.
Love,
Rani

questions.passage: Yawning is one of the most common behaviours in the animal kingdom, yet scientists still cannot fully explain it. The old idea was that yawning brings extra oxygen to the body, but experiments showed that people yawned just as often in rooms with more oxygen. A newer theory suggests that yawning helps cool the brain. A deep breath draws in cooler air and increases blood flow, which lowers brain temperature. This might explain why people yawn more in warm weather than in freezing cold. Another mystery is that yawning is contagious: seeing someone yawn can make us do the same. Researchers believe this may be linked to empathy, since children under four rarely catch yawns.

The garden now grows spinach, tomatoes and chilli, and each family who helped may harvest vegetables free of charge. Extra produce will be sold at the Saturday market, and the money will be used to buy seeds and tools. "We wanted a place where neighbours can meet, not just a place to grow food," said coordinator Bu Lestari. The school also plans to use the garden as an outdoor classroom for science lessons beginning next semester.

options: They will be used only by the volunteers.
They will be sold to buy seeds and tools.
They will be given to the school canteen.

questions.passage: It was 10.45 p.m. when Dimas realised he had missed the last bus. The station was almost empty, and a cold wind pushed an empty can across the floor. He checked his phone: 3 percent battery. His mother would be worried, but he could not call her. Then he noticed an old man sweeping the platform. "Missed it, boy?" the man asked. Dimas nodded. Without a word, the man took out a small phone from his pocket and handed it over. "Call your family. Then wait with me. My nephew is coming with his truck, and we pass your village anyway." Dimas looked at the stranger's kind eyes and felt his shoulders relax for the first time that evening.

The old man took his phone.
He did not know her number.

questions.passage: Inflation is a general rise in prices over time. When inflation is 5 percent a year, something that costs Rp100,000 today will cost about Rp105,000 next year. This means that money buys less than before. Economists say that a small and stable level of inflation is normal in a growing economy, but sudden increases can cause hardship, especially for families who spend most of their income on food. Several factors can cause inflation. When demand for goods grows faster than supply, sellers raise prices. Higher production costs, such as expensive fuel, may also push prices up. To control inflation, central banks usually raise interest rates, which makes borrowing more expensive and encourages people to save rather than spend.

questions.passage: Coral reefs cover less than one percent of the ocean floor, yet they support about a quarter of all marine species. In recent decades, however, rising sea temperatures have caused "bleaching", a condition in which corals lose the colourful algae living inside them and turn white. Bleached corals are not dead, but they are weak and may starve if the water does not cool quickly. Pollution and overfishing add to the problem. Some scientists are now growing heat-resistant corals in laboratories and transplanting them onto damaged reefs. Others call for stronger limits on carbon emissions. They argue that unless global warming slows down, even the most resilient corals will not survive in the long term.

questions.passageTitle: The Life of Ki Hajar Dewantara
questions.passage: Ki Hajar Dewantara was born in Yogyakarta in 1889 as Raden Mas Soewardi Soerjaningrat. As a young man he worked as a journalist and wrote sharp articles criticising Dutch colonial rule. One of them, titled "If I Were a Dutchman", led to his exile in the Netherlands in 1913. There he studied education and became convinced that schools should respect the natural talents of children. After returning home, he founded the Taman Siswa school in 1922, which offered education to local children who were not allowed to attend Dutch schools. He later served as Indonesia's first Minister of Education. His birthday, 2 May, is now celebrated every year as National Education Day.
questions.text: Why was Ki Hajar Dewantara sent into exile?
questions.explanation: Artikel kritisnya "If I Were a Dutchman" membuatnya diasingkan.
options: He wrote an article that criticised colonial rule.
He opened a school for Dutch children.

questions.passage:
Subject: Request to Hold a Recycling Week
Dear Mr. Haryanto,
I am writing on behalf of the Environmental Club to propose a Recycling Week at our school from 3 to 7 March. During this week, students would bring used plastic bottles, paper, and cans to special collection points in the school yard. Each class would be given points based on the weight of materials collected, and the winning class would receive a plant for its classroom. We would also invite a local waste bank to give a short talk on how recycling can create jobs. We believe this activity will increase environmental awareness and reduce the waste produced by our canteen. We hope you will consider our proposal.
Yours sincerely,
Nabila Putri
Chair, Environmental Club

To announce the winner of a competition

questions.passageTitle: How to Make Perfect Rice Without a Rice Cooker
questions.passage: Many people think a rice cooker is essential, but a simple pot works just as well. First, rinse one cup of rice in a bowl until the water runs almost clear; this removes extra starch that makes rice sticky. Next, put the rice in a pot and add one and a half cups of water. Bring it to a boil over high heat, then immediately reduce the heat to the lowest setting and cover the pot with a tight lid. Do not lift the lid for 15 minutes, because the steam inside cooks the rice. After 15 minutes, turn off the heat and let the pot rest for another five minutes. Finally, loosen the rice with a fork before serving.

questions.passageTitle: The Fox and the Fisherman's Net
questions.passage: A hungry fox once found a fisherman's net lying on the riverbank. Inside it were three fat fish. "What a lucky day!" he thought, and he began to pull them out. Suddenly, the net tightened and trapped his paw. The fox cried out in pain. A passing crow landed beside him and said, "Brother Fox, you were too greedy. If you had taken only one fish, you could have escaped." The fox hung his head. "I wanted everything and now I have nothing," he sighed. The crow felt sorry for him and, with its sharp beak, loosened the knot. The fox ran away, limping, and from that day he never took what did not belong to him.

The net tightened around his paw.

questions.passageTitle: Smartphones in the Classroom: Help or Hindrance?
questions.passage: Should students be allowed to use smartphones in class? Many teachers say no. They point to a study in which students who kept their phones on their desks scored lower on a test than those whose phones were in a bag, even when the phones were silent. According to the researchers, the mere presence of a phone divides attention. Yet banning phones completely may not be the answer. Phones can be useful tools for looking up words, taking photographs of the whiteboard, or running science experiments. A better solution might be clear rules: phones may be used only when the teacher allows, and must be put away at other times. This balance helps students benefit from technology without losing focus.

questions.passage: The cheetah can run at speeds of up to 100 kilometres per hour, making it the fastest land animal. Its body is built for speed: long legs, a flexible spine, and a small head reduce air resistance, while large nostrils help it take in oxygen quickly. However, this speed comes at a price. A cheetah can sprint for only about 30 seconds before overheating, and it needs half an hour to recover. During that time, other predators such as lions or hyenas may steal its prey. Because of this and habitat loss, only about 7,000 cheetahs are left in the wild. Conservationists therefore work to protect grasslands and to reduce conflict between cheetahs and farmers.
questions.text: Why can a cheetah sprint for only about 30 seconds?

options: It needs oxygen from the water.

questions.passage: In a world full of fast news and short videos, reading a novel can feel old-fashioned. Yet research suggests that people who read fiction regularly are better at understanding other people's feelings. When we follow a character's thoughts for hundreds of pages, we practise looking at the world through someone else's eyes. This skill, known as empathy, is valuable at school, at work, and in friendships. Fiction also builds vocabulary and attention span, because it demands that we stay with a single story for a long time. This does not mean that every novel is helpful, nor that non-fiction is useless. However, setting aside even twenty minutes a day for a good story is a small habit with lasting rewards.

questions.passageTitle: Teenagers and Social Media: A Parent's View
questions.passage: My fifteen-year-old daughter spends nearly four hours a day on social media, and I used to worry constantly. Last month, instead of taking her phone away, I asked her to show me what she was watching. To my surprise, much of it was educational: videos about drawing, English grammar and even coding. She also keeps in touch with cousins who live far away. This does not mean that social media is harmless. Some content is unsuitable, and sleep suffers when phones stay in bedrooms. So we made a family agreement: no screens at the dinner table, and all phones charge in the living room at night. Conversation, not punishment, turned out to be the most effective approach.

questions.passage: Stretching for more than 21,000 kilometres, the Great Wall of China is often described as the only man-made structure visible from space. In fact, astronauts have said that it is extremely hard to see with the naked eye, because it is narrow and the same colour as the surrounding land. The wall was not built at one time, either. Different dynasties built and repaired sections over more than two thousand years, mainly to protect against invasions from the north. Many parts were made of rammed earth, while the famous stone sections near Beijing were built during the Ming dynasty. Today, the wall attracts millions of tourists each year, but some remote parts are crumbling because of weather and human damage.

questions.passage: A volcanic eruption can be terrifying, yet the land around volcanoes is among the most fertile in the world. Ash and lava contain minerals such as phosphorus, potassium and iron. Over time, weather breaks these materials down and mixes them with soil, creating a rich layer that supports crops. This is why farmers in Java and Bali plant rice, coffee and vegetables on the slopes of Mount Merapi, Mount Bromo and Mount Agung, despite the danger. However, fertility is not a guarantee of safety. Authorities set up warning systems and evacuation routes, and farmers must follow official advice. In this way, communities can enjoy the benefits of volcanic soil while reducing the risk.

questions.passage: Every weekend, sixteen-year-old Salsa spends three hours at an animal shelter, washing dogs and cleaning cages. At first, she joined only because her school required community service. "I thought it would be boring," she admits. Yet after a few months, she began to look forward to every visit. She learned patience from the nervous dogs, and she discovered that she enjoys talking to adopters. Last month, she helped find a home for a one-eyed puppy that nobody wanted. questions.passageTitle: Water Scarcity: A Growing Global Crisis
questions.passage: Although two-thirds of the planet is covered by water, only about 3 percent is fresh, and most of that is frozen in glaciers. Today, more than two billion people lack access to safe drinking water. Population growth, pollution and climate change are making the problem worse. In many regions, farmers use up to 70 percent of the available fresh water for irrigation, often wasting it through old, leaking systems. Experts suggest several solutions: repairing pipes, using drip irrigation, recycling waste water and collecting rainwater. Nevertheless, technology alone cannot solve the problem. Individuals must also learn to value water by closing taps, shortening showers and refusing to pollute rivers.

questions.passage: Indonesia lies on the Pacific "Ring of Fire", so earthquakes are a part of life. Knowing what to do can save lives. If you are indoors when the shaking starts, drop to your hands and knees, cover your head and neck under a sturdy table, and hold on until the shaking stops. Do not run outside, because falling glass and bricks are the biggest danger. If you are in bed, stay there and protect your head with a pillow. If you are outdoors, move away from buildings, trees and power lines. After the shaking stops, check yourself for injuries, turn off gas and electricity, and prepare to leave if the building is damaged. Always keep an emergency bag with water, a flashlight and first-aid supplies near the door.

questions.passage: Jakarta and Bandung are only 150 kilometres apart, but they feel like different worlds. Jakarta, the capital, is a busy business hub with skyscrapers, heavy traffic and a population of more than ten million. Bandung, in contrast, sits in a cool highland and is famous for its fashion shops, cafés and creative communities. While Jakarta offers more jobs in finance and government, Bandung is popular among students and artists because of its universities and relaxed pace. Both cities face challenges: Jakarta struggles with floods and congestion, whereas Bandung has problems with rubbish and growing traffic on weekends. The new high-speed train now connects the two cities in about forty minutes, making it easy for people to enjoy the best of both.

questions.passage: Every morning, thousands of teenagers drag themselves to school at 6.45 a.m., half asleep. Research shows that during adolescence the body clock shifts, so most teenagers naturally fall asleep after eleven o'clock and need about nine hours of sleep. When classes start too early, they simply cannot get enough rest. The result is poor concentration, bad moods and lower grades. Some schools that moved their start time by an hour reported fewer absences and better test scores. Critics argue that later schedules would disturb parents' work and after-school activities. These concerns are valid, but they can be solved through planning. Surely the health and learning of students should come first.

questions.passage: Deep in the ocean, where sunlight cannot reach, many creatures produce their own light. This phenomenon is called bioluminescence. It occurs when chemicals inside an animal's body react with oxygen, creating a cold blue or green glow. Animals use light in different ways. The anglerfish dangles a glowing lure to attract prey, while some squid release a cloud of glowing liquid to confuse predators, much as other squid release black ink. Fireflies on land use flashes to find mates. Scientists are studying these chemicals to create safer medical tests and even street lamps that need no electricity. Perhaps the future of lighting lies in the dark depths of the sea.
questions.text: How does bioluminescence occur?
options: Chemicals in an animal's body react with oxygen.

questions.passage: One of every three bites of food we eat depends on pollination, and bees do most of the work. As a bee flies from flower to flower collecting nectar, grains of pollen stick to its body and are carried to the next flower, which allows fruit and seeds to form. Almonds, apples, blueberries and coffee are just a few of the crops that need bees. Unfortunately, bee populations are falling around the world because of pesticides, disease, and the loss of wildflowers. Some farmers now leave strips of wildflowers beside their fields and use fewer chemicals. Households can help too, by planting flowers on balconies or in gardens. If bees disappear, our meals would become far less varied and much more expensive.

questions.passageTitle: From the Diary of a First-Time Climber
questions.passage: Saturday, 6 April. I thought I was fit until the third hour of the climb. My legs trembled, my backpack felt like a bag of bricks and the air grew thin. The guide, Pak Ujang, told us to breathe slowly and take small steps. "The mountain is not a race," he smiled. At 4.30 a.m., we reached the summit just before sunrise. A sea of clouds spread below us, glowing orange. I forgot my sore muscles and almost cried. Looking at the horizon, I realised how small my worries about exams and friendship drama were. On the way down, I promised myself that I would climb again next year – with better shoes.
questions.text: What advice did the guide give?
options: Breathe slowly and take small steps

questions.passageTitle: Is Online Shopping Better Than Going to the Mall?
questions.passage: Online shopping has exploded in recent years, and it is easy to see why. Shoppers can compare prices in seconds, read reviews from other buyers and have items delivered to their doors. For people who live far from big cities or who have difficulty walking, it is a huge benefit. Nevertheless, buying online has risks. Photos can be misleading, delivery may be delayed, and returning products is sometimes complicated. Malls, by contrast, allow customers to touch and test goods and to enjoy a day out with friends. For the best results, many consumers combine both: they research online, then visit a shop to check the product before buying.
questions.text: Which is an advantage of online shopping?

questions.passage: Nina had been postponing her dental appointment for months. When she finally sat in the chair, her hands were cold with fear. Dr. Siska smiled and explained each step before she touched anything. "If it hurts, just raise your hand and I'll stop immediately," she said. The treatment was shorter than Nina had expected, and she felt only slight pressure. Afterwards, Dr. Siska showed her how to brush properly, using a plastic model of teeth. "Brush twice a day for two minutes, and don't forget to floss," she advised. Nina left the clinic relieved and a little embarrassed. She had wasted months worrying about something that was not nearly as terrible as she had imagined.

| Appliance | Hours used per day | Electricity (kWh/month) |
|---|---|---|
| Air conditioner | 8 | 120 |
| Refrigerator | 24 | 45 |
| Television | 5 | 15 |
| Washing machine | 1 | 10 |

The air conditioner uses the most electricity, accounting for 63 percent of the total. Mr. Hartono plans to reduce the monthly bill by setting the air conditioner to a higher temperature and using it for only six hours a day. He also wants to unplug the television when it is not in use because devices on standby still consume power.

questions.passage: Walk through any Indonesian city at night and you will see them: stray cats searching for food among rubbish bins. Their number is increasing because they reproduce quickly; one female can have up to three litters a year. Many of them suffer from hunger, disease and traffic accidents. Some residents feed the cats regularly, but this alone does not solve the problem and may even attract more strays. Animal welfare groups recommend a method called TNR: Trap, Neuter and Return. The cats are caught, sterilised, vaccinated and then returned to their territory. Over time, the population stabilises without cruelty. Cities that adopted TNR report fewer cats and less conflict between neighbours.

questions.passage: In the village of Tirtomulyo, a typhoon ripped the roof off the community hall last year. The village head, Pak Slamet, gathered everyone at dawn. Farmers brought bamboo, women prepared food, and teenagers carried tiles from house to house. The hall was rebuilt in just nine days, faster than any contractor could have done it. "No one was paid," Pak Slamet said, "yet everyone worked as though the hall belonged to them – because it did." This tradition, known as gotong royong, has existed in Indonesia for centuries. In an age when many people are absorbed in their own lives, the story of Tirtomulyo reminds us that shared effort is still one of our greatest strengths.

questions.passage: Of the 7,000 languages spoken in the world, about half are expected to disappear by the end of this century. Indonesia, home to more than 700 regional languages, is particularly affected: some, like those in Papua and Maluku, are spoken by fewer than a hundred people. When a language dies, a unique way of understanding the world is lost, including traditional stories, medical knowledge and place names. Linguists suggest several measures: teaching regional languages in primary schools, recording elders' speech, and creating digital content such as apps and songs. Young people play a vital role, since a language survives only if it is spoken by the next generation. Preserving a mother tongue does not mean rejecting national or global languages; it means keeping our heritage alive.

questions.passage: In temperate countries, leaves turn red, orange and yellow every autumn. The explanation lies in chemistry. During spring and summer, leaves are green because they contain chlorophyll, a pigment that absorbs sunlight to make food for the tree. When days grow shorter and cooler, the tree stops producing chlorophyll. As the green fades, other pigments that were hidden all along become visible: yellow and orange carotenoids. Red leaves are different. Their colour comes from anthocyanins, which are made fresh in autumn when sugars are trapped in the leaves. Bright, sunny days and cool nights produce the most spectacular reds. In tropical countries such as Indonesia, where seasons are less distinct, most trees keep their leaves green throughout the year.

questions.section: Teks Visual-Ringkas, Percakapan, dan Teks Campuran
questions.passage: In temperate countries, leaves turn red, orange and yellow every autumn. The explanation lies in chemistry. During spring and summer, leaves are green because they contain chlorophyll, a pigment that absorbs sunlight to make food for the tree. When days grow shorter and cooler, the tree stops producing chlorophyll. As the green fades, other pigments that were hidden all along become visible: yellow and orange carotenoids. Red leaves are different. Their colour comes from anthocyanins, which are made fresh in autumn when sugars are trapped in the leaves. Bright, sunny days and cool nights produce the most spectacular reds. In tropical countries such as Indonesia, where seasons are less distinct, most trees keep their leaves green throughout the year.

questions.passage: Sales of electric vehicles (EVs) have grown rapidly in the past decade. Supporters point out that EVs produce no exhaust fumes and, therefore, improve air quality in crowded cities. They are also cheaper to run: electricity costs less than petrol, and electric motors have fewer parts that need repair. Nevertheless, there are obstacles. EVs are still more expensive to buy, and charging stations are scarce outside large cities. Moreover, if the electricity comes from coal, the overall benefit for the climate is smaller than it appears. For EVs to truly help the environment, governments must invest in both charging networks and renewable energy. Only then can the promise of cleaner transport be fulfilled.

questions.passage: Long ago, a poor boy named Malin lived with his mother in a fishing village. Determined to change his fate, he left on a merchant ship, promising to return. Years later, he came back as a rich man with a beautiful wife and a grand ship. His mother ran to the shore, weeping with joy. But Malin, ashamed of her ragged clothes in front of his wife, pushed her away and said, "I do not know this old woman!" Heartbroken, she prayed to God. Suddenly a storm rose, and Malin's ship was smashed. He and his ship were turned to stone. To this day, the people say the rock on the shore is Malin Kundang, a reminder to respect one's parents.

He wanted to change his fate.

questions.passage: Every second, the equivalent of one rubbish truck of clothing is burned or buried in a landfill. This is the result of "fast fashion", a business model in which cheap clothes are made quickly and sold in huge quantities to follow the latest trends. Producing a single cotton T-shirt requires about 2,700 litres of water – the amount a person drinks over two and a half years. In addition, the dyes used in factories often pollute rivers. Consumers can make a difference by buying fewer, higher-quality items, repairing damaged clothes and donating or reselling unwanted garments. Some young people have started "swap parties", where friends exchange clothes instead of shopping. These small actions may seem trivial, but together they can slow the demand that drives fast fashion.

| Kupang | 380 | 330 | 260 | 90 |

questions.passage:
Reporter: Rina, you started your own business at seventeen. How did it begin?
Rina: It began in the kitchen. I loved baking, and my friends kept asking for my cookies, so I started selling them at school.
Reporter: What was the biggest challenge?
Rina: Managing time. I had to bake at night and still complete my homework. Some nights I only slept four hours.
Reporter: How do you handle that now?
Rina: I hired two part-time helpers and made a schedule. Now I sleep eight hours.
Reporter: What advice would you give young people?
Rina: Start small, but start. And don't be afraid of failure. My first batch of cookies was burnt, and look where I am now.

questions.section: Teks Visual-Ringkas, Percakapan, dan Teks Campuran
questions.passage: In 2018, a small village football team in Flores unexpectedly won the district championship, defeating clubs with far more experienced players. Their coach, Pak Yohanes, believed that talent was less important than trust. Every Friday, instead of practising only drills, the players cooked dinner together and talked about their week. On the pitch, they passed the ball quickly because they knew what their teammates would do. "We had no star," Pak Yohanes explained, "but we had eleven people who would run for each other." Sports psychologists say this is common: teams with strong bonds communicate better under pressure and recover faster from mistakes. The lesson reaches beyond sport, to classrooms and workplaces as well.
questions.text: Why was the team's victory surprising?
